name: Guardian genius crossword No 258
preamble: Related features are omitted from wordplay in half the clues. Wordplay in other clues indicates an additional letter in each. The additional letters can be arranged to identify the related features.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Getting into performing

blocks.note: performing a task is doing it
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: Someone getting into acting, taking up performing as a career.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the thirteen clues whose wordplay leaves out the doubled letters: DOING plus the double N gives DONNING.
explanation.definitionFit: To don clothes is to put them on, so getting into a coat is donning it.

clue.text: Fabric producer cutting rubbish flowers

indicators.note: a thing cutting another slices into its middle, so it sits inside

blocks.note: BS is slang shorthand for nonsense or rubbish
a loom weaves cloth
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: A textile mill's waste is choking the local flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds BLOOMS, itself a synonym; restoring the double S gives BLOSSOMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Blossoms are the flowers on a tree or shrub, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Undercoats look brilliant

indicators.note: split in two, its second half says coats, and a coat goes round whatever it covers

blocks.note: sub- is the Latin prefix for under
to peer is to look closely

explanation.surface: Fresh undercoats of paint make the walls look brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undercoats' must be split into Under and coats. The wordplay gives SUPEERB; one of the extra-letter clues, its spare E goes towards DOUBLE LETTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb and brilliant are both words of high praise for excellent things.

clue.text: One interrupts, requesting leader removed for taking off

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and removing it drops that letter
something that interrupts breaks into the middle of what is going on

blocks.note: requesting something is asking for it
the Roman numeral for one
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: Someone butts into a conversation, asking for a turn to speak before taking off.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives SKIING; the doubled M is the missing feature.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimming milk means removing the cream from its surface, so it is a kind of taking off.

clue.text: Fruit drinks

blocks.note: ales are pints of beer
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: Fruit drinks, as on a café menu.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, juice; split it into definition and wordplay. ALES with the double P restored gives APPLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Apples are the commonest orchard fruit, so the plural noun matches.

clue.text: State Sibyl, needing no introduction, also breaking wind

indicators.note: an introduction is what comes first, so without it the opening letter goes
breaking into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine
a sibyl was a prophetess of the ancient world, a seer
and means also, in addition

explanation.surface: An oracle bursting in unannounced while someone breaks wind.
explanation.walkthrough: ME plus EER broken by AND gives MEEANDER; this is an extra-letter clue, and the spare E goes towards the hidden message. 'Breaking wind' is a joke: wind is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A river or path that winds turns back and forth, which is what meander means as a verb.

clue.text: Launch uniform adopted by foundation

indicators.note: something adopted is taken in, so it ends up inside the other piece

blocks.note: the root is the base something grows from
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet, and also the abbreviation
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: A charity's new uniform is being launched.
explanation.walkthrough: Without its doubled L the wordplay spells a non-word, a sign this clue lacks a feature.
explanation.definitionFit: A rollout is the public introduction of a new product or service, its launch.

clue.text: Captain Scarlet at first given vat

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: only the first letter is kept
a kier is a vat for boiling or bleaching cloth
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: Captain Scarlet, the puppet hero of a 1960s British TV series, being handed a vat.
explanation.walkthrough: S plus KIER gives SKIER; restoring the double P gives SKIPPER. Kier is a rare word solvers mostly meet in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipper is the captain of a boat or a sports team.

clue.text: Catholic tore off manufacturer of goodies

indicators.note: off here means gone wrong or awry, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Catholic storming out of a sweet factory.
explanation.walkthrough: The twelve letters of Catholic tore give the eleven of the answer with a spare T; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A chocolatier makes chocolates, which are sweet treats or goodies.

clue.text: Nobody's missing top that is comfortable clothing

indicators.note: the top of an across word is its first letter, and missing it means losing that letter

blocks.note: nobody's is no one's
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Nobody is going topless, though it would be comfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: No one's without its N plus IE gives OONESIE, with one spare O; this is an extra-letter clue. Reading nobody as NONE gives the answer with no spare, a trap.
explanation.definitionFit: A onesie is a loose one-piece garment worn for lounging, so it counts as comfortable clothing.

clue.text: Engineer old and humane found in country

indicators.note: to engineer is to construct or contrive, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An engineer, old and kind, discovered living abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine letters of old and humane give the eight of the answer with a spare U; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A homeland is the country a person or people comes from.

clue.text: Lundy mostly round and open

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: Lundy is an island in the Bristol Channel
the letter O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Lundy island is mostly flat and open ground.
explanation.walkthrough: LUND plus O gives LUNDO, with a spare L; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a knot or a parcel is to open it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Sick beau arranged old papers

indicators.note: to arrange is to put things in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: A lovesick boyfriend sorting through a pile of old newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: Sick beau has eight letters; the answer has ten because the doubled S is the missing feature.
explanation.definitionFit: Back issues are earlier editions of a newspaper or magazine, so they are old papers.

clue.text: Prophet revealing artists' log or designs

indicators.note: as a verb, designs means plans or lays out afresh, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seer whose visions are revealed in a painter's notebook or sketches.
explanation.walkthrough: Twelve letters of fodder give eleven of the answer with a spare R; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrologist claims to foretell events from the stars, a kind of prophet.

clue.text: Irish centre perhaps strips

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the letters in the middle are kept

blocks.note: the middle three letters, spelt out in words as 'R, I and S'
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: An Irish rugby centre, perhaps, stripping off.
explanation.walkthrough: The centre of IRISH is RIS, and 'perhaps' asks for it written as a list, R, I AND S. Add the double B for RIBBANDS. 'Centre' first suggests a rugby position.
explanation.definitionFit: Ribband is an old spelling of ribbon, and also a strip of timber in shipbuilding.

clue.text: Satisfied welcoming European with sharp teeth

indicators.note: to welcome a guest is to take them in, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: sated means satisfied, full
E is the abbreviation for European
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: A well-fed host welcoming a European guest, with a sharp-toothed grin.
explanation.walkthrough: E inside SATED makes SEATED; restoring the doubled R gives SERRATED.
explanation.definitionFit: A serrated edge, like a bread knife's, has a row of small sharp teeth.

clue.text: One who's sticking together, increasingly sad

blocks.note: someone who glues things together is a gluer
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: Someone who sticks with a partner, though growing sadder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticking together' looks like loyalty; read literally it is applying glue. The wordplay gives GLUER, and the double M restores GLUMMER.
explanation.definitionFit: Glum means gloomy, and the comparative glummer is sadder, more and more so.

clue.text: Cheated and left hurriedly about 1

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: to flee is to leave in a hurry
I is the Roman numeral for 1
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: A swindler who cheated and fled in a hurry, around one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: '1' looks like a reference to 1 Down but is just the numeral. I inside FLED gives FILED, then the double D.
explanation.definitionFit: To fiddle is to swindle or falsify accounts, so fiddled is past-tense cheated.

clue.text: Two bishops visiting foreign caliphate in progressive order

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's place
something foreign is strange and unfamiliar, so the letters are put into an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: B is the chess notation for bishop, so two make BB
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two senior clergy visiting a caliphate in some far-off land.
explanation.walkthrough: Eleven letters of fodder give ten of the answer, with one spare B; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Alphabetic order runs steadily from A to Z, so it progresses in sequence.

clue.text: Coloured skirt seen in the past

definitions.note: the past tense of skirt, a verb

blocks.note: hued means having a colour
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: A coloured skirt glimpsed long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirt' looks like the garment; it is the verb, and 'seen in the past' puts it in the past tense. HUED plus the double G gives HUGGED.
explanation.definitionFit: A road that hugs the coast keeps close beside it, so hugged and skirted are synonyms.

clue.text: Bacterial fuel

blocks.note: coal is burnt as fuel
the preamble's double letter, left out of the wordplay and restored in the grid

explanation.surface: Fuel contaminated by bacteria.
explanation.walkthrough: COAL with the double C restored gives COCCAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Coccal relates to cocci, round-shaped bacteria such as streptococci.

clue.text: Part of dress drops

blocks.note: the train is the long back part of a gown that trails on the ground

explanation.surface: A detail of a gown drops down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' suggests a hidden word, but no answer hides in 'dress'. The wordplay gives TRAIN, with a spare T; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain falls in drops of water, so the noun drops can mean rain.

clue.text: Blunt, shortly annoy and go away

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: Emily Blunt is a British film actress
something that grates irritates you

explanation.surface: Someone telling another bluntly to stop annoying them and go away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunt' looks like an adjective, but it is the actress's surname. EMIL plus GRATE gives a spare L; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To emigrate is to leave one's country to live elsewhere, a permanent going away.

clue.text: Leaves firm investing in discs

indicators.note: investing in means putting into, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: CDs are compact discs
firm means hard, solid

explanation.surface: A company quitting its investment in a record business.
explanation.walkthrough: The firm goes in straight after the first letter of the discs, so their D survives as a spare letter; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Chard is a leafy green vegetable, so its leaves are chards.

clue.text: Stars show butts on stages

blocks.note: the stages of a journey or a tour are its legs
cigarette butts are their ends

explanation.surface: Celebrities flash their backsides on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, A on B puts A after B. The plural stages keep their S, a spare letter; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A legend is a famous, celebrated performer, a star.

clue.text: One is preparing food to recreate pie

definitions.note: read as one who is preparing food, a noun

indicators.note: in printing, pie is type that has been spilt and jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook is attempting to remake a pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pie' looks like the dish; it is the printer's word for jumbled type. RECREATE has a spare E over the answer; this is an extra-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A caterer supplies and prepares food for events.
